title: Designing Agents (The Floor Is the Frontier) — Ben Hylak, Raindrop

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary:
Ben Hylak opens by noting that despite the track being titled continual learning, real-world continual learning is scarce. A year ago, agents barely existed and products were mostly chatbots where evals were simple fact-checking exercises—you knew the answer to most user questions. Now agents are deployed in finance, healthcare, and defense, and their creativity cuts both ways: they find ingenious solutions but also do catastrophically unexpected things. Hylak argues most eval advice remains stuck in the chatbot era—prescribing thousand-example eval suites that break as soon as you switch models or harnesses (e.g., moving to Claude Code CLI breaks 80% of evals). He advocates for safety without theater, cautioning against investing months in eval sets that slow you down.

Hylak represents Raindrop, which finds critical production agent issues, verifies fixes, and simulates changes pre-deployment. The core question he reframes is not 'what issues does your agent have'—since agents have effectively infinite issues—but 'how do you make it better.' He distinguishes benchmark maxers from floor raisers and notes that companies and labs have different jobs. He introduces the ceiling/floor distinction: the ceiling is the most impressive emergent capability; the floor is the worst behavior—like recommending a competitor, deleting data, or sending AI slop to a customer—which is what breaks trust.

For offline evals, Hylak argues they should look like code tests (unit tests, e2e tests), not prompt playgrounds, because the prompt is now the whole harness—all the code, connections, and logic. He references Sentry's Vitest evals package and OpenAI's 'macro evals' as examples. For raising the floor, you need to discover unknown issues and, for each issue, know two things: when it started and what percent of users it affects. Knowing something started yesterday triggers investigation of what changed; knowing it hit three users versus a hundred thousand tells you whether to care. He also notes the approach radically differs by user count—at millions of messages per day, experiments on free-tier samples are extremely valuable; with five users, they are not.

Hylak shares three tactical lessons from Raindrop. First, clusters are not issues: clustering traces is useful for one-off analysis but doesn't scale because boundaries drift, you don't control them, what counts as one issue is product-specific, and a cluster like 'price issues' merges a wrong quote with a wrong refund that have different root causes. Second, code mode scales to traces: write classifiers and run them in a sandbox at production volume. Third, agents are very bad at anomaly detection but good at investigating anomalies—so surface deterministic signals like keyword frequency spikes first, then hand them to an agent to investigate.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Raising the floor and the reality of continual learning
sections.summary: Hylak opens by noting continual learning is rare in real-world products and proposes a practical, dialogue-driven session about what actually works for making agents better, inviting audience questions.

sections.title: Agents a year ago vs now: creativity cuts both ways
sections.summary: A year ago agents barely existed and products were chatbots with simple fact-checking evals. Now agents are deployed in finance, healthcare, and defense. Their creativity makes them powerful but also catastrophically unpredictable.

sections.title: Eval advice stuck in the chatbot era
sections.summary: Most eval advice online prescribes thousand-example eval suites that break when models or harnesses change. Switching to Claude Code CLI broke 80% of evals. Hylak advocates safety without theater.

sections.title: Raindrop, Workshop, and howtoeval.com
sections.summary: Hylak introduces Raindrop (production agent issue detection, like Sentry for agents), Workshop (open-source tracing tool for self-healing loops used by thousands), and howtoeval.com (a no-bullshit guide to agent evaluation).

sections.title: The real question: how to make your agent better
sections.summary: The core question is not what issues your agent has—since it has potentially infinite issues—but how to make it better given the tools available, balancing what to solve now vs waiting for model improvements.

sections.title: Benchmark maxer vs floor raiser and labs vs companies
sections.summary: Hylak distinguishes benchmark maxers from floor raisers and notes labs and companies have different jobs. Labs build general-purpose models; companies imbue domain-specific knowledge. The word 'eval' is overloaded and confusing.

sections.title: Responsibility varies by product and the ceiling/floor framing
sections.summary: Responsibility varies by product shape—from copilot autocomplete where users delete errors, to Devin where user setup matters, to AI doctors with very different stakes. Hylak introduces the ceiling (best emergent capability) and floor (worst behavior) distinction, noting the floor is what breaks trust.

sections.title: Floor examples and offline evals as code tests
sections.summary: Hylak gives concrete floor examples—recommending a competitor, deleting data, sending AI slop email to a customer—and says the floor breaks user trust. He argues offline evals should look like code tests (unit tests, e2e tests), not prompt playgrounds, because the prompt is now the whole harness. He references Sentry's Vitest evals and OpenAI's macro evals as examples.

sections.title: Two numbers per issue and user count matters
sections.summary: For raising the floor, you need to discover unknown issues and know two things per issue: when it started and what percent of users it affects. Knowing it started yesterday triggers investigation of what changed; knowing it hit three users vs a hundred thousand tells you whether to care. Approach differs radically by user count—experiments work at millions of messages per day but not with five users.

sections.title: Lesson one: clusters are not issues
sections.summary: Clustering traces is useful for one-off analysis but doesn't scale: boundaries drift, you don't control them, what counts as one issue is product-specific, and clusters like 'price issues' merge a wrong quote with a wrong refund that have different root causes. You also can't reliably track clusters over time.

sections.title: Lesson two: code mode scales to traces
sections.summary: Code mode, known in the context of MCPs, scales to traces: you write classifiers and run them in a sandbox at production volume. Hylak highly recommends trying this approach.

sections.title: Lesson three: agents cannot spot anomalies
sections.summary: Agents are very bad at anomaly detection but good at investigating anomalies. Pull out deterministic signals like keyword frequency spikes—something tangible that an agent can then investigate. Hylak closes by inviting attendees to find him after the talk for conversation rather than formal Q&A.
